html:
The Battle of Thymbra was fought in the winter of 547 or 546 BCE on a plain near Sardis, in the west of today's Turkey. Cyrus the Great of Persia beat King Croesus of Lydia, and then took Sardis after a short siege.

Croesus, famous for his wealth, had crossed the river Halys to attack the new Persian power. After a drawn battle at Pteria he went home and sent his allies away for the winter. Cyrus did not wait. He followed at once and met the Lydians outside their capital. Herodotus says he put camels in front of his line, because their smell frightened the Lydian horses, and so broke their famous cavalry. Croesus fled into Sardis, which fell after about fourteen days.

Lydia became a province of the Persian Empire, and so did the Greek cities of the Aegean coast that Croesus had ruled. This brought Persia face to face with the Greeks for the first time. The sources are Herodotus and Xenophon, and Xenophon's account of the battle is partly invented. Seven years later Cyrus took Babylon.
